subject: Re: TTFT & streaming SLOs — next steps / PoC

Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>

Subject: Quick follow-up on today's call — TTFT & streaming

Hi Marissa / Aditya,

Thanks for the demo earlier — the team found Redwood's streaming behavior promising. I wanted to capture the performance targets we discussed and get confirmation that those are achievable for our workload before we lock in the PoC scope.

Key targets from our side:
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT): <= 200ms P95 from request arrival to first token byte at our edge.
- Concurrency: sustained 50 concurrent user sessions, burst to 150 for short windows.
- Throughput: roughly 500 inference requests/sec during peak, average ~200 rps.
- Streaming: server-sent events (SSE) preferred, WebSocket OK. We expect chunk cadence of approximately 150–300ms between meaningful chunks for normal responses.

Payload & token context: average input size ~1.2k chars (~250 tokens), responses ~80–150 tokens.

Can you confirm these numbers look reasonable, and outline the next steps for the PoC (what we'll need from us, what Redwood will run, expected timeline)? Also please attach any short spec you use for TTFT measurements so we can align.

Thanks,
Samir
Director of Product
FinServe AI

Subject: Re: Quick follow-up on today's call — TTFT & streaming

Samir — great to connect today, and thanks for summarizing. Quick recap + proposed next steps below.

Recap / definitions (to make sure we're aligned):
- TTFT (Time-to-first-token): we measure from the time the request reaches Redwood's ingress (HTTP/SSE/WebSocket) to the first data byte emitted to the client. For streaming endpoints this excludes client-side network latency.
- Target: <= 200ms at P95 is achievable for this workload in our hosted offering assuming average model context and average token lengths you listed. We'll validate during the PoC.
- Streaming transport: we support SSE and WebSocket. SSE is generally simpler for browser clients; WebSocket may be slightly more efficient for many small bi-directional messages.
- Chunk cadence: we aim to batch/generate tokens to emit every ~150–300ms for typical responses; exact cadence depends on model, prompt length, and the runtime batching window.
- Concurrency / throughput: sustaining 50 concurrent sessions with 500 rps peak is within a typical Dedicated capacity profile. We'll size the PoC to mirror your concurrency/throughput and measure queues and queuing latency.

Tradeoffs and notes:
- Lower TTFT often requires smaller batching windows or pinned capacity (dedicated or reserved). If you prioritize P95 TTFT <=200ms over cost, we recommend a dedicated pool for the PoC.
- Chunk cadence is influenced by the model's per-token compute and our batching — very short cadence (<100ms) can reduce efficiency and raise cost.

Requested from FinServe for PoC:
1) Sample request payloads (one-line and long prompt examples) — you mentioned you could share a CSV with examples.
2) Preferred transport (SSE vs WebSocket) and any client-side constraints (browser, mobile SDK, edge proxies).
3) Target test window and dates for the PoC (we suggest a 2-week run with a dedicated pool for final verification).

What Redwood will deliver for PoC:
- A dedicated test pool sized to reproduce concurrency and peak throughput.
- Measurement dashboard with TTFT P50/P90/P95, chunk cadence histogram, per-request token counts, and backend CPU/GPU utilization.
- A short report with tuning recommendations (batching window, quantization, autoscale policy).

Proposed timeline:
- Today/Tomorrow: you share sample payloads + confirm transport.
- Wed (2027-08-11): Redwood provisioning & baseline run.
- Next Mon (2027-08-16): start 2-week PoC.

I've attached a short proposal that outlines how we measure TTFT and the PoC acceptance criteria (redwood-ttft-slo-proposal.pdf).

If that sounds good, I'll open the HubSpot PoC record and loop in infra to provision the pool.

Cheers,
